tip: 'Varken ... eller' is the fixed pair for neither ... nor: 'varken han eller hon'. Use 'eller' here, not 'och'.
'Kommer att' + infinitive expresses predictions, especially weather and external events: 'det kommer att regna'.
'Istället för att' takes an infinitive: 'istället för att vänta' = instead of waiting, not instead of to wait.
'Ska' marks a planned future event: 'vi ska gifta oss' means we are getting married.
For hypotheticals Swedish uses the past tense: 'om jag var du' means if I were you, literally if I was you.
'Inte bara ... utan också' frames not only ... but also; here 'också' follows the verb: 'utan förberedde också presentationen'.
An adverb like 'redan' normally sits between 'har' and the main verb: 'har redan ätit', not 'har ätit redan'.
'Springande' (running) keeps one form no matter the noun: verb forms in '-ande' or '-ende' never change shape.
When the owner is clear from context, Swedish often uses the definite form instead of a possessive: 'har förlorat passet', not 'sitt pass'.
The '-s' on 'ses' means each other: 'vi ses' is we see each other, the everyday way to say see you.
When a clause like 'så länge du är här' (as long as you're here) opens the sentence, the verb comes before the subject: 'är jag glad', not 'jag är glad'.
'Berätta' needs 'för' before the listener: 'berättade för mig' means told me. You cannot drop the 'för'.
For a length of time Swedish normally uses 'i': 'bott i två år' means lived for two years, not 'för'.
'Klaga' takes 'över' before what you complain about: 'klagade över att' means complained that.
Reported speech normally uses past perfect ('hade fått') when the original statement was past tense ('fick').
Unlike English, Swedish past participles change like adjectives: 'en stängd dörr', 'ett stängt hus', 'den stängda dörren'.
Present participles like 'leende' (smiling) end in '-ande' or '-ende' and keep one form no matter the noun.
'Öronbedövande' is literally ear-deafening: Swedish often builds vivid compounds from a noun plus a verb form.
'Just' here means just now. It sits between 'har' and 'kommit' to say something happened moments ago.
The small word 'upp' changes the verb: 'ringa' alone means to call, and 'ringer upp' means to phone someone up, here to call back.
'Vart' means where to, for direction. 'Var' means where something sits. 'Vart vinden blåser' asks which way.
'Säga åt någon att' means tell someone to do something: 'sa åt mig att vänta'. Don't drop the 'åt'.
In an indirect question where the question word is the subject, add 'som': 'vem som hade ringt', not 'vem hade ringt'.
Swedish says 'ha rätt', literally have right, to mean be correct: 'han hade rätt', he was right.
'Anställd' (employed) can act as a noun: 'de anställda' means the employees, no separate word for people needed.
Open the sentence with a phrase like 'enligt honom' and the verb comes next, before the subject: 'var det', not 'det var'.
'Under all kritik' literally means below all criticism: something so bad it is beyond critiquing at all.
After 'uppmanade', put the object 'oss' first, then 'att lämna'. Pattern: urge someone 'att' plus the verb.
Swedish can drop the noun after 'den' plus an adjective: here 'den blå' means the blue one, with no noun needed.
'Det sägs att' means it is said that – a common way to report a claim without naming who says it.
